transfer_card.item: Traction and sinkage on target, thermal control, dust adhesion, radiation on electronics
Getting stuck or sinking in loose soil
transfer_card.note: tested on Earth, never predicted. On the Moon the soil itself weighs less and grips less, so Earth sand holds the rover better even with a lightened twin: VIPER twin slipped 42 % at 30 deg on Earth vs 85 % simulated on the Moon (arXiv 2405.11001). Every Earth result is optimistic.

transfer_card.item: Abrasive wear of wheels, seals and bearings
transfer_card.note: tested on Earth, never predicted. Lunar regolith has angular, glassy grains not rounded by wind or water; Apollo dust wore suits, seals and mechanisms within days. Rounded Earth sand underestimates wear; young volcanic or pyroclastic ground is closer (see wear_test_hint).

notes: Gates act on slope averaged over the baseline in the feature name; local slopes inside a cell are steeper. Prefer a p90 slope column for the gate when it exists.
No slip, sinkage, traction or maximum climbable slope is predicted for the Moon or Mars.
Tolerances and gates are only valid for the baseline in their names; 5 km slopes are much gentler than 300 m slopes.

thermal_inertia_class has no product at the lunar south pole: it is NaN there and its weight is redistributed. Lunar polar regolith is always fine and loose, so soil class only discriminates for Mars.
Loose-soil analog sites are wanted, not avoided: getting stuck on Earth is cheap, on the Moon it ends the mission.
Abrasive wear is not scored. Use wear_test_hint() on each named site: volcanic/pyroclastic sites are better for wear tests, loose sediments give optimistic wear results.

Before the pitch, check the ranking with validate_rover_ranking(): Bardenas must make sense for rover (BASEPROD rover dataset at Bardenas Reales, Gerdes et al., Scientific Data 11:1054 (2024), doi:10.1038/s41597-024-03881-1).
